overview.intro: Grammar in the ISC examination is not a memory test of labels; it is a test of control under transformation. The candidate who can turn a statement into a question, a direct speech into reported speech, or an affirmative into a negative without changing meaning owns the underlying structure rather than a rule recited. This chapter builds that ownership in four moves: the mechanics of sentence transformation with its fixed patterns; tense consistency across a paragraph; phrasal verbs and prepositions, where native-feeling usage is decided; and error correction, which trains the eye to see what the ear misses. The chapter closes with the commonest examination traps — agreement, ellipsis and misplaced modifiers — each with the diagnostic that exposes it.

learningOutcomes: Transform sentences across degrees, voices, speech types and question forms without altering meaning.
Maintain tense consistency through paragraphs and justify every tense switch.
Use phrasal verbs and prepositions accurately in formal and informal registers.
Diagnose and repair agreement, ellipsis and modifier errors in continuous prose.
Apply transformation patterns to tag questions, conditionals and reported questions.

learn.title: Transformation: fixed shapes for changing meaning-preserving

blocks.text: Transformation asks one question in a hundred disguises: how do I say the same thing differently without changing what it means? Each subtype has a fixed machinery the examiner expects to see executed exactly. Degrees of comparison move positive to comparative to superlative with their attendant than and the, and the transformation must preserve scope — “one of the best” cannot become “the best”. Voice moves subject and object across the verb and forces the tense to survive the trip: the auxiliary is rebuilt to match the original tense, and the participle takes the form of the main verb. Direct to reported speech shifts pronouns and backshifts the tense one step into the past, while the time and place markers move with the reporting verb: now becomes then, here becomes there. Interrogatives invert the auxiliary back, keep wh-words for wh-questions and use whether or if for yes/no reported questions. Finally, tag questions compress the whole grammar of the sentence into three words: the tag reverses the polarity of the statement, repeats its auxiliary, and matches the pronoun.

items: Comparative: -er / more + than; superlative: -est / most + the; preserve quantifiers like one of the.
Passive: object becomes subject, auxiliary rebuilt to the original tense, main verb in participle.
Reported speech: pronoun shift, one-step backshift, now → then, here → there.
Yes/no questions report with whether or if; wh-questions keep their wh-word.
Tag: reverse polarity, repeat the auxiliary, match the pronoun; am becomes aren’t in tags.
Imperatives report as told, asked, ordered or requested someone to, plus the bare infinitive.

items.note: The work has been finished by her — auxiliary has survives, been is added, finished stays a participle.
He asked whether I finished at four — the yes/no question takes whether and the tense backshifts.
He suggested that we begin — the hortative takes suggested plus a that-clause with the base verb.

blocks.caption: Transformation patterns at a glance
rows: using main verb in the tag

blocks.text: A paragraph lives in one time frame until a reason forces a change, and examiners read for the seams. The default for narrative is the simple past: every finite verb belongs to it, and habitual actions in that past take used to or would rather than repeated simple pasts that sound jerky. Reported sentences backshift one step, so a present fact reported in a past narrative takes the past form even though the fact remains true: “He said he was tired” describes a present state through a past reporting verb. Two legitimate reasons escape the frame: a general truth stays present — “the teacher said the earth revolves” — and a past perfect appears only to signal the earlier of two past events. Continuous forms mark duration inside the frame rather than leaving it. The diagnostic is underlining every finite verb in a draft and checking that each one belongs to the paragraph’s frame or carries a stated reason for departure.

items: Underline every finite verb; each must sit in the paragraph’s time frame or have a stated reason.
Habitual past: used to or would, not a string of simple pasts.
Reported speech backshifts one step; present facts may stay present after said that.
Past perfect appears only to order two past events: the earlier one takes had + participle.
General truths keep the present tense inside past narration.
Continuous forms mark duration: was walking, had been waiting, have been trying.

items.text: Slip: “He opened the door and sees the room empty.”
items.note: Two frames collide; sees becomes saw, restoring the simple-past narrative.

items.text: Correct past perfect: “The train had left when we reached the platform.”
items.note: Two past events, one earlier: had left orders them without extra words.

items.meaning: The one-step movement of tenses when a sentence is reported.
The controlling time frame a paragraph’s verbs must share.
A verb describing a state rather than an action, normally unfaked.
had + past participle, marking the event earlier than another past event.

blocks.text: Phrasal verbs are idiomatic units whose meaning is not the sum of their parts: look after does not mean look while caring, give up does not mean give upward, and run into means meet by chance. Each carries its own preposition or adverb, and the particle cannot be swapped without changing or destroying the meaning — look for is search, look up is consult or improve, look after is care for. Prepositions behave the same way at the level of the single verb: arrive at a place but arrive in a country, insist on a thing but insist that a person do something. Precision also governs the register split: write to someone and ring someone up belong to ordinary usage, while formal writing prefers inform, contact or telephone, and phrasal verbs with a casual sound should be avoided in reports and proposals. The examination tests these choices directly and through error correction, where the wrong particle is the planted slip.

items: The particle is part of the meaning: look up, look for, look after are three different verbs.
Separable phrasal verbs take the object in the middle: hand in the report / hand the report in.
Inseparable ones never split: run into a friend, not run a friend into.
Prepositions are idiomatic: arrive at / in, insist on / that, good at, capable of.
Formal register prefers single-word verbs: inform rather than tell, contact rather than ring up.
A changed particle changes the verb: put off postpones, put up with tolerates, put out extinguishes.

items.text: “The meeting was put ____ because of the rain.”
items.note: put off — postpone; put up (accommodate), put out (extinguish) and put away (store) all fit the noun but not the meaning.

items.text: Register slip: “Please ring me up with your decision, sir.”
items.note: In a formal letter: “Please inform me of your decision at your convenience.”

learn.title: Error correction: agreement, ellipsis and modifiers

blocks.text: Error correction rewards the writer who can name the disease before prescribing the cure, and three diseases account for most planted slips. Agreement binds the verb to its subject, but the subject is sometimes disguised by a prepositional phrase — “the box of records is”, not are — or by a conjunction joining two nouns that share one article, “bread and butter is”, because the pair names a single dish. Ellipsis removes words that are understood, and the pronoun that remains must still match: “each of the students has”, because each is singular no matter what follows the of-phrase. Modifiers must sit next to what they modify, and a dangling modifier opens a sentence its subject never performs: “Walking to school, the rain began” claims the rain was walking. The repair is to place the modifier beside its intended noun or recast the sentence so the correct noun performs the action. Each correction should be written as a rule the sentence now obeys, which is exactly how the examiner’s rubric is phrased.

items: Ignore the of-phrase: look at the head noun — each, every, one of the students takes singular.
Compound subjects with one article name one thing: bread and butter is.
Dangling modifiers attach to the wrong noun; recast so the true subject performs the action.
Neither … nor agrees with the nearer subject; either … or behaves the same way.
Collective nouns take a singular verb when the group acts as one body.
State the rule after the repair — the mark follows the rule, not just the corrected word.

items.text: “The box of old letters were heavy.”
items.note: Head noun box is singular: was heavy; the of-phrase does not control agreement.

items.text: “Having finished the essay, the television was switched on.”
items.note: Dangling modifier: “Having finished the essay, she switched on the television.”

items.meaning: The noun a prepositional phrase or qualifier attaches to, which controls agreement.
The omission of words understood from context, leaving a pronoun to match.
An opening participle whose sentence never gives it the right subject.
A noun naming a group acting as one unit, taking a singular verb.

keyPoints: Transformation preserves meaning exactly; the machinery for each subtype is fixed.
Passive rebuilds the auxiliary to the original tense and keeps the participle.
Reported speech backshifts one step and moves time and place markers.
Tags reverse polarity, repeat the auxiliary and match the pronoun.
One time frame per paragraph; underline finite verbs to police the seams.
Past perfect exists to order two past events, nothing else.
Phrasal verbs are idiomatic units; the particle cannot be swapped.
Formal register prefers single-word verbs to casual phrasal verbs.
Agreement follows the head noun, not the nearest noun.
Dangling modifiers attach to the wrong noun — recast so the true subject acts.
examFocus: In transformation, execute the pattern fully: tense, pronoun and marker all move together.
Name the rule in error correction; marks follow the stated rule, not only the fix.
Watch quantifiers: one of the, each of the and neither of the decide singular or plural.
Reported questions keep statement word order — no inversion survives the backshift.

vocabulary.meaning: The one-step pastward movement of tense when speech is reported.
A three-word clause appended to a statement, reversing its polarity.
A verb plus particle forming an idiomatic unit with its own meaning.
The adverb or preposition that completes a phrasal verb and fixes its sense.
The noun controlling agreement when qualifiers and phrases surround it.
The understood omission of words, leaving pronouns to carry the reference.
An opening modifier whose sentence never gives it the correct subject.
A verb expressing a state rather than an action, normally resistant to continuous forms.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct tag: “Everyone has finished, ____?”
questions.explanation: Indefinite pronouns like everyone take a plural tag with they, since the tag’s pronoun must match the understood people.

questions.prompt: Which sentence keeps the time marker correct when reported? “I will meet you here now,” she said.
options: She said she would meet me there then.
She said she will meet me here now.
She said she would meet me here now.
She said I would meet her here then.
questions.answer: She said she would meet me there then.
questions.explanation: will backshifts to would, here moves to there and now moves to then — all three markers must travel.

questions.prompt: The sentence “The box of supplies ____ heavy” takes:
questions.explanation: The head noun box is singular; the of-supplies phrase does not control the verb.

questions.prompt: Which particle completes “The committee ____ the proposal after three hours of debate”?
questions.explanation: Turn down means reject, which suits a debate’s outcome; turned up means arrive or increase and turned over means transfer or consider.

questions.prompt: The one-step pastward movement of tenses when speech is reported is called __________ .
questions.explanation: Backshift moves present to past and will to would when the reporting verb is in the past.

questions.prompt: An opening participle whose sentence never supplies the right subject is called a __________ modifier.
questions.explanation: A dangling modifier attaches to the wrong noun, producing an unintended and often comic reading.

questions.prompt: Transform to the passive without changing meaning: “The committee has approved the new timetable.”
questions.answer: The new timetable has been approved by the committee. The object moves to subject position, the auxiliary has is retained because the original tense must survive the change, been is inserted to carry the perfect, and approved remains the past participle; the original subject becomes the agent with by.
questions.explanation: The passive preserves tense exactly while exchanging grammatical roles.

questions.prompt: Rewrite as a reported question: “Where have you put the files?”
questions.answer: He asked me where I had put the files.
questions.explanation: A wh-question reports with its wh-word kept, the statement word order restored, the pronoun shifted to me and the tense backshifted one step from present perfect to past perfect.

questions.prompt: Explain why “Neither the teacher nor the students ____ present” takes a plural verb, while “Neither the students nor the teacher ____ present” takes a singular one, and state the general rule.
questions.answer: With neither … nor and either … or joining two subjects, the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it — the rule of proximity. In the first sentence students stands next to the verb, so the plural are present is correct; in the second the teacher is nearer, so was present is correct. The rule exists because the construction presents alternatives one at a time rather than as a combined unit, so the verb must match whichever alternative has just been named. This differs from and, which joins subjects into a single compound normally taking a plural, and from collective nouns, which take a singular when the group acts as one body. Recognising which conjunction binds the subjects therefore decides the verb before the meaning is even considered.
questions.explanation: Proximity governs correlative conjunctions; and builds compounds and collectives act as units.

questions.prompt: A candidate writes: “Having reviewed the reports, the recommendations were accepted by the board.” Identify the error, explain why examiners penalise it, and rewrite the sentence two different ways.
questions.answer: The opening participle Having reviewed dangles: its understood subject must be the body that performed the review, but the sentence’s grammatical subject is the recommendations, which cannot review anything. Examiners penalise it because the opening modifier is where the reader forms the first connection between clause and subject, and a mismatch there creates a momentary misreading that the sentence never repairs; the rubric files it under grammatical accuracy and clarity of expression together. The first repair restores the true subject: “Having reviewed the reports, the board accepted the recommendations.” The second removes the participle entirely and states the action as a finite clause: “After the board had reviewed the reports, it accepted the recommendations.” Both versions keep the original order of events while attaching the reviewing to the only body capable of it.
questions.explanation: The dangling participle is marked under grammatical accuracy because the opening clause sets an expectation the subject cannot satisfy.
